opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
The readings today circle around one theme: thirst, and the condition of the human heart. In the desert between Massah and Meribah the Israelites are physically thirsty, but the deeper problem is trust. They ask the devastating question, “Is the Lord in our midst or not?” Psalm 95 takes that moment in Israel’s history and turns it into a warning for every generation: “If today you hear His voice, harden not your hearts.” The issue is not the lack of water; it is the tendency of the human heart to doubt God even when He has already shown His presence.

Paul answers that ancient doubt directly in Romans. If anyone wonders whether God is truly with us, the cross settles the question. “While we were still sinners Christ died for us.” God did not wait for humanity to become worthy. His love was proven when we were still far from Him. The distrust voiced in the desert finds its answer in the sacrifice of Christ.

The Gospel then brings us to another place of thirst: Jacob’s well in the town of Sychar in Samaria. That place itself carries centuries of history. The land had been given to Joseph, Jacob’s son, and Joseph’s bones were later buried there. The well stood as a memory of the patriarchs and of the mercy Joseph once showed his brothers who had betrayed him. For the Samaritans this place represented their claim to the ancient heritage of Israel. That history explains the woman’s words when she asks Jesus, “Are you greater than our father Jacob who gave us this cistern and drank from it himself with his children and his flocks?” She knows the story of Jacob. She knows the inheritance connected to Joseph. She also knows the expectation shared throughout the region: “I know that the Messiah is coming.”

Yet she also stands within a long and complicated history. After the fall of the northern kingdom, foreign peoples were brought into Samaria and their worship mixed with the traditions of Israel. Ancient sources even describe five foreign deities introduced into the land. When Jesus tells the woman, “You have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband,” He is revealing her personal life, but many readers have also noticed how strikingly it mirrors the spiritual history of Samaria itself — a people whose worship had been divided and incomplete.

That is why the conversation immediately turns to the deeper issue: worship. “Our ancestors worshiped on this mountain,” she says, “but you say that the place to worship is in Jerusalem.” Jesus answers by acknowledging the history of the covenant: “You worship what you do not understand; we worship what we understand, because salvation is from the Jews.” The Messiah comes through Israel. Yet something greater is now arriving. “The hour is coming, and is now here, when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth.” Worship will no longer depend on a mountain in Samaria or a temple in Jerusalem. The place of encounter with God will move from geography to the human heart.

Throughout the conversation Jesus speaks in images of thirst and hunger. He offers the woman living water that becomes a spring within a person. When the disciples urge Him to eat, He answers with another mystery: “I have food to eat that you do not know about. My food is to do the will of the one who sent me and to finish his work.” What sustains Him is obedience to the Father and the completion of the work of redemption.

What is remarkable is that Jesus reveals His identity here with unusual clarity. To this Samaritan woman — someone outside the religious boundaries of Israel — He openly says, “I am he, the one speaking with you.” The one who arrived at the well thirsty becomes the first to recognize the living water. She leaves her jar, returns to the town, and tells the people, “Come see a man who told me everything I have done.” Through her testimony many come to believe. In this way the woman who came searching for water becomes the first messenger carrying news of the Messiah to Samaria.

In the end the entire thread of Scripture comes together at that well. In the wilderness the people asked, “Is the Lord in our midst or not?” At Jacob’s well the answer is standing before a woman drawing water. The Messiah Himself says, “I am he, the one speaking with you.” The God whom Israel questioned in the desert is now present in the flesh, offering living water to anyone willing to receive it. And the warning still echoes for every generation: if today you hear His voice, harden not your hearts.
